blocks.manuscript: Bringing agricultural needs into our project

blocks.body: NemaKlear explores early warning for agricultural nematode risks through engineered yeast that recognizes candidate ascaroside signals and produces a visible color response. Alongside building this system, we need to ask: Who would use such a test? When would testing help guide crop management? What could the signals in soil, and the resulting color, tell us? These questions connect Human Practices with our research goals, validation conditions, and proposed testing workflow.

We brought our project into farm visits, expert interviews, public surveys, and conversations with companies, then brought their perspectives back into team discussions. Growers showed us how testing needs depend on local crops and production conditions. Plant protection and soil researchers helped us connect early detection with pre-planting decisions and examine signal interpretation, sample representativeness, and background interference. Public and business perspectives drew our attention to handling, interpretation, storage, and cost. Together, these exchanges helped us define a clearer use case and more specific questions to investigate.

This work also produced practical resources. Our soil collection initiative brought together samples from different backgrounds, while sampling guidance and records connected field conditions with future research. Lessons, picture books, and project presentations helped us explain agricultural problems and biosensing to different audiences. Discussions about participant rights, engineered-yeast safety, and continuity beyond the season encouraged us to consider responsibility throughout engagement, research, and future use.

This page follows the connections between project questions, stakeholder feedback, team responses, and further validation. Investigation documents fieldwork, soil collection, interviews, and team exchanges; Education presents our teaching and public communication work. Here, we explain how those experiences helped refine NemaKlear’s research questions and intended use. Explore Investigation → Explore Education →

blocks.text: Field visits and agricultural advice: who needs a test, and when?

blocks.body: Underground disease can be difficult to recognize, while yellowing, wilting, or poor growth may have several causes. Through farm visits and consultations with agricultural specialists, we explored where early warning could help with practical decisions.

On June 6, our discussion with Yurong Yao at the Tianjin Academy of Agricultural Sciences helped us understand hidden root damage and the handling and cost barriers to testing. Visits to growing sites in Tianjin also revealed local differences: nematodes were not the most urgent problem in every field. The value of testing needed to be considered alongside crops, field history, and management plans.

On August 18, Qian Liu at China Agricultural University reminded us that testing before above-ground symptoms appear could still miss a useful management window. Pre-planting screening became an important setting for discussing the project’s value. “Early” began to mean something more specific: when to collect a sample, which decision the result should inform, and how long a user could wait.

blocks.text: Public questionnaire: what do people know about nematodes, and what do they want from a test?

blocks.body: We designed a questionnaire covering nematode awareness, agricultural impacts, attitudes toward control methods, and expectations of testing. We wanted to understand how respondents viewed the problem and how we could explain our project more clearly.

We collected 369 responses, with self-reported locations spanning 23 provincial-level regions. Of these respondents, 197 (53.4%) had never heard of plant-parasitic nematodes or knew the term without understanding the details. This gave our educational work a starting point: explain nematodes and their hidden damage before introducing the sensor.

For an ideal testing tool, 261 respondents selected ease of use (70.7%), 208 selected accuracy and reliability (56.4%), and 199 selected affordability (53.9%). Respondents could choose up to three features; all percentages use 369 responses as the denominator. We connected these expectations with practical questions about sample preparation, controls, interpretation, storage, and total cost.

Most respondents were students or worked in research or education, with more responses from Shandong and Tianjin. We considered their views alongside growers’ experiences and expert advice. The findings also informed lesson design, connecting our needs research and science communication around the same agricultural problem.

blocks.text: Expert interviews: what can a detected signal tell us?

blocks.body: During expert interviews, we introduced our proposed path from ascaroside recognition to a color response in yeast and invited plant protection and soil researchers to examine it. A central question emerged: what could a detected signal tell us?

Qian Liu asked whether signal differences could support the proposed interpretation and how detecting a compound related to identifying nematodes or estimating their density. This helped us distinguish signal detection, composition analysis, density estimation, and risk assessment, and consider the evidence needed at each step.

Zhihao Pang at Beijing Forestry University raised questions about soil processes. If ascaroside #3 and ascaroside #18 degrade at different rates, would their measured proportions still reflect the original signal? How might soil background color affect the readout? These questions brought environmental conditions into our discussion of both input and output.

Together with Liu’s advice to progress from simpler conditions to real samples, these interviews clarified the need to examine signal stability, background controls, and sample conditions. They gave our wet-lab and dry-lab teams concrete questions to discuss: how should modeling assumptions relate to sample conditions, and what evidence is needed to connect color responses with agricultural risk? The modeling and Engineering pages present the corresponding technical analyses and progress. Explore Engineering →

blocks.text: The soil collection initiative: how can field conditions enter our research?

blocks.body: Understanding soil variation requires actual samples. Expert advice on differences between plots, representative sampling, storage, and processing also drew our attention to the information accompanying each sample.

Through our soil collection initiative, we gathered 289 samples from nine provincial-level regions, covering different cropping backgrounds and environmental settings. Sample identifiers were linked to location, crop, collection date, and management history so that subsequent discussions could refer back to the conditions of origin.

We prepared a standard operating procedure for soil collection, packaging, transport, and biosafety, together with a guidance video and workflow diagram. These resources connected recordkeeping, multi-point sampling, sealing, temporary storage, transport, and laboratory handling. They supported participants during collection and gave the team a shared basis for receiving and managing samples.

The initiative turned field participation into traceable research materials and a documented workflow, supporting future comparisons of soil backgrounds, color interference, and sample preparation. Nematodes and chemical signals within these samples still require identification and measurement. Investigation provides the sample overview and workflow details. Explore Investigation →

blocks.text: Corporate outreach: how do we explain the project’s value to potential users?

blocks.body: Surveys and expert discussions repeatedly raised ease of use, reliable interpretation, and affordability. This encouraged us to consider portability across the entire process, from sampling and preparation to reaction, interpretation, and disposal, as well as storage and transport. Corporate outreach added another perspective on these conditions of use.

To seek support and opportunities for discussion, we prepared a partnership invitation and project presentation. These materials brought together the agricultural problem, research progress, potential users, and the support we hoped to receive. Preparing and presenting them prompted us to explain the technology through practical situations: who might need it, how it could help, and what using it would involve.

As students without a business background, we gained a first-hand sense of entrepreneurial thinking: explaining value, understanding another party’s concerns, and considering what it takes to move research toward application. Discussions about cost, storage, and product format helped us reconsider possible use by agricultural input companies, large farms, and crop protection service providers. Sponsorship from ExCell Bio also provided practical support for our research and participation in iGEM.
These experiences helped us see that a testing tool’s value must be considered within a workflow its users can manage. Future real-sample studies and user feedback will help refine that positioning.

blocks.text: Education and team exchanges: how do we explain and advance the project responsibly?

blocks.body: Lesson design, public communication, and exchanges with other teams gave us opportunities to revisit how we explained the project. We needed to describe how color was produced and how signal interpretation related to agricultural risk. Lessons and picture books built around “input—sensing—output” helped us practice clearer explanations. Education presents these materials and their use. Explore Education →

Team exchanges also made questions of responsibility more concrete. At the US-China Human Practices Summit on August 30, questions about questionnaire ethics review and continuity beyond the season encouraged us to consider participant rights, information management, and future use.

Expert safety concerns brought these discussions back to practical handling. Pang raised the possibility of engineered-yeast leakage and the need for post-test treatment, prompting us to consider safe disposal alongside convenience. Our soil sampling and laboratory receipt procedures addressed handling requirements through the relevant SOP. Together, these perspectives encouraged us to examine responsibilities across data collection, research communication, and future application.

blocks.text: Bringing feedback together: what can we build on next?

blocks.body: Across these activities, pre-planting screening gave early warning a more specific setting. Expert interviews clarified questions about signal interpretation and real-sample validation. Soil collection established materials and procedures, while public and corporate engagement added considerations about handling, cost, and communication. These perspectives helped refine both NemaKlear’s research direction and its intended use.

blocks.body: Our questionnaire and statistical notes, sampling standard operating procedure, sample records, teaching materials, and outreach documents provide a foundation for continued work. Other teams can draw on the question design, sampling organization, and communication approaches, adapting them to their own agricultural settings.

The next step is to keep real-sample studies and feedback on the complete workflow connected to the project: examine how soil backgrounds affect responses, assess preparation and interpretation conditions, and understand the difficulties users encounter. These questions will guide our continuing assessment of how an engineered-yeast sensor could serve agricultural testing.
